newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - HK's David Tang muses handover to China.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK's David Tang muses handover to China.

text.p: Flamboyant businessman David Tang -- club owner, socialite, friend of film stars and minor British royals -- pulls deeply on his trademark Cuban cigar and muses over the British colony's imminent return to Chinese rule.
"One foot cannot straddle two boats," he says in clipped British tones, exhaling a plume of hazy blue smoke towards the ceiling of his office graced with oil paintings and antiques.

But contrary to the ancient Chinese proverb, and like so many of Hong Kong's elite, Tang, 43 is the offspring of a marriage between Chinese and British cultures, a porridge of differing loyalties with a uniquely Hong Kong flavour.
Chinese by birth, British by education, Tang -- founder of the upmarket China Club and the chic Shanghai Tang department store -- is insouciant about the change ahead.

Chinese rule will bring together the extremes of communism and laissez-faire capitalism, and this will complicate the process, says Tang. But Hong Kong will adapt, tone down its critical voice and find new ways to profit.

"I think because the sovereign is a communist regime, people will become much more conscious of self-censorship, and I think Hong Kong will go on thriving and become alright because of this self-censorship," he says matter-of-factly.
Before, Hong Kong people cultivated and nurtured connections with the British governor and a royal here or there.
"Now the sucking-up is the same, but it's a bit more difficult to be good friends with communists because they're very wary of the political files on them," Tang says.
CHINA IS, AFTER ALL, THE MOTHERLAND
People, foreigners, frequently confuse the motherland with communism, he says. The tie is one of blood, of nationhood, of common roots and a shared heritage.
"I can't explain it any other way than this biological thing called blood. That bears out there is this huge feeling of going back to the motherland," Tang says.

"Before, it might be a bit awkward for the Chinese in Hong Kong to be shouting for the Union Jack to go up at the Olympics, now there's absolutely unequivocal loyalty to China with the five-star flag, even though its a communist country," he said.
Hong Kong's glittering rise from barren rock to one of the world's great financial cities is testimony to British rule.
"If there was ever a shining star, a shining example of colonialism, it's Hong Kong: perhaps colonialism should not be got rid of," he says.

"I suspect that the Chinese were absolutely staggered by the fact that the British did not fight for the retention or the extension of the lease, or some diluted version of the return of sovereignty," says Tang.
Tang can indirectly trace his Jardine House office to the roots of colonialism in Hong Kong.

A century and a half ago, prominent China coast merchant William Jardine urged British Foreign Secretary Lord Palmerstone to send in the gunboats. Britain's spoils of victory in the so-called Opium Wars was Hong Kong, seized at gunpoint.
Tang defends the colony's 28th and last British governor, Chris Patten, hated by China for introducing democratic reform.
"I don't think it's fair to blame Chris Patten, because after all it was the Hong Kong Legislative Council, properly elected itself, that passed the political package," he said.
CHINESE ROOTS
These seemingly conflicting views are easily explained, since Tang's past is closely entwined with Hong Kong's history.

"I was born here," Tang says. "My great grandfather came to Hong Kong first, lots of people came across the border at the turn of the century, he was Cantonese and I suppose he was a refugee in a way."
In 1933, Tang's grandfather founded Kowloon Motor Bus, whose blue-and-white double deckers still ply the streets.
"When everybody started wearing Western clothes, my grandfather started wearing Chinese gowns," Tang said. "He was always in Chinese flowing gowns or Chinese traditional jackets."
An old Who's Who shows Sir Tang Shiu-kin, philanthropist, sporting the high collar of a Chinese gown. He is listed as being born in 1901, in Hong Kong. His nationality, British.
Tang junior is wearing wide flapping sleeves, traditional collar and buttons in the style of China's 10th Century courts.

Hong Kong's was a rocky road to riches, and amidst the left-wing inspired riots and bloodshed of 1966 and 1967, the adolescent David left for Britain with his mother, part of the first generation of young people to go abroad to study.
"It was terrible arriving in England," Tang grimmaces. "I couldn't speak a word of English."

As the only Chinese boy in a British boarding school, Tang felt like "a chimpanzee behind bars in a zoo". But helpful teachers, luck and ingenuity saw him master English and graduate from the University of London with a degree in philosophy.

Tang's first marriage was to a Hong Kong Chinese woman he met in the early 1980s. Now he is set to wed a young British woman he met at a dinner party he threw seven years ago for British cabinet minister Michael Heseltine.
"She is the kind of person you feel completely comfortable with," he says, grinning.
